s: the suitors plot to murder Telemachus (during his return from Pylos and Lacedaemon)
q: They are going to try and murder Telemachus as he is coming home from Pylos and Lacedaemon, where he has been to get news of his father.

s: Antinous is a ringleader of the suitors (foremost among them)
q: Antinous and Eurymachus, who were their ringleaders and much the foremost among them all, were sitting together when Noemon son of Phronius came up and said to Antinous,

s: Antinous is son of Eupeithes
q: When they came, Antinous son of Eupeithes spoke in anger.

s: Antinous is angry Telemachus's journey to Pylos and Lacedaemon (strongly)
q: Good heavens, this voyage of Telemachus is a very serious matter; we had made sure that it would come to nothing, but the young fellow has got away in spite of us, and with a picked crew too.

s: Antinous commands the suitors' plot to kill Telemachus (as its leader)
q: Find me a ship, therefore, with a crew of twenty men, and I will lie in wait for him in the straits between Ithaca and Samos; he will then rue the day that he set out to try and get news of his father.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK I.
s: Apollo sends a plague upon the Achaeans because Agamemnon dishonors Chryses by refusing to return Chryseis. Calchas reveals the cause, and Agamemnon agrees to release Chryseis but demands another prize, leading to a bitter quarrel with Achilles over Briseis. Minerva prevents Achilles from killing Agamemnon, but Achilles swears to withdraw from the fighting, and Agamemnon sends men to take Briseis. Chryseis is sent back to Chryses with sacrifices for Apollo, while the plague-stricken Achaeans purify themselves and offer hecatombs.

Achilles calls the Achaeans into assembly, accepts Calchas’s account of Apollo’s anger, and argues that Agamemnon must return Chryseis without ransom. He fiercely rebukes Agamemnon for threatening to take Briseis, nearly attacks him, but restrains himself when Minerva commands him to do so. He then declares that he will no longer fight and returns to his tents and ships.

Agamemnon refuses Chryses’s ransom and keeps Chryseis, bringing Apollo’s plague upon the Achaeans. After Calchas identifies the cause, Agamemnon agrees to return Chryseis but demands another prize and threatens to take Briseis from Achilles. He sends Chryseis away with a hecatomb and orders Talthybius and Eurybates to bring him Briseis.

The Achaeans suffer from Apollo’s pestilence, with many people dying and funeral pyres burning throughout the host. They gather in assembly, support respecting Chryses and accepting his ransom, purify themselves, and offer sacrifices to appease Apollo. Their leaders’ quarrel disrupts their unity, and Achilles refuses to fight with them.

The Trojans are fighting the Achaeans in the war, but they are not responsible for Achilles’ grievance against them. Achilles says that they have not raided his cattle or horses or destroyed his harvests. They would rejoice if they heard Agamemnon and Achilles quarreling.

Apollo becomes angry because Agamemnon dishonors his priest Chryses. He sends a pestilence against the Achaeans, shooting his arrows first at their mules and hounds and then at the people. He will not end the plague until Chryseis is returned and a holy hecatomb is offered at Chryse.

Chryses comes to the ships of the Achaeans carrying a ransom and the sceptre of Apollo, asking for the release of his daughter Chryseis. Agamemnon rejects and insults him, so Chryses prays to Apollo to avenge his tears. He is to receive Chryseis back when the Achaeans send her to Chryse.

Chryseis is held by Agamemnon after he refuses the ransom offered by her father, Chryses. To appease Apollo, Agamemnon sends her back to Chryse with a hecatomb and places Ulysses in command of the voyage.

Briseis is Achilles’ prize, awarded to him by the sons of the Achaeans. Agamemnon threatens to take her as compensation for surrendering Chryseis and later sends Talthybius and Eurybates to seize her. Achilles allows Patroclus to hand her over, while declaring that the act will have consequences if the Achaeans later need his help.

Jove’s counsels are said to be fulfilled through the deaths caused by the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles. Calchas says that dreams come from Jove, and Agamemnon claims that Jove, the lord of counsel, will support him. Nestor says that Agamemnon’s greater authority comes from having more people under him by Jove’s favor.

l: the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles, The Iliad, BOOK I.
s: The quarrel begins when Agamemnon refuses to release Chryseis unless he receives another prize. Achilles accuses him of greed and injustice, while Agamemnon threatens to take Briseis from Achilles. Minerva prevents the conflict from becoming physical, but the quarrel leads Achilles to refuse further fighting.

l: Achilles' withdrawal from the war, The Iliad, BOOK I.
s: Achilles declares that he will return to Phthia and later swears that the Achaeans will seek him in vain when they are suffering. After Agamemnon takes Briseis, Achilles goes back to his tents and ships with Patroclus and his company. He refuses to fight for the Achaeans unless they later seek him and cannot find him.

l: plague among the Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK I.
s: A plague strikes the Achaeans after Apollo hears Chryses’s prayer. It lasts for nine days, killing people as well as mules and hounds, and fills the host with funeral pyres. The Achaeans purify themselves and offer sacrifices after learning that the plague will end only when Chryseis is returned and Apollo is appeased.

l: Achilles’ anger, The Iliad, BOOK I.
s: Achilles’ anger is directed chiefly at Agamemnon for dishonoring him and threatening to take Briseis. His rage nearly leads him to draw his sword and kill Agamemnon, but Minerva restrains him. He continues to denounce Agamemnon and swears that the Achaeans will regret driving him from the fighting.

l: Apollo's pestilence, The Iliad, BOOK I.
s: Apollo’s pestilence is sent against the Achaeans because Agamemnon has dishonored Apollo’s priest. Apollo shoots his arrows among the host for nine days, causing widespread death. Calchas says that it will continue until Agamemnon returns Chryseis and sends a holy hecatomb to Chryse.

l: Chryseis' release and return to Chryses, The Iliad, BOOK I.
s: Agamemnon agrees to release Chryseis after Calchas explains that Apollo’s plague is punishment for keeping her. He sends her aboard a ship commanded by Ulysses, together with a hecatomb for Apollo, so that she may be returned to Chryses at Chryse.

l: the Trojan War, The Iliad, BOOK I.
s: The Trojan War has brought the Achaeans to fight against the Trojans and to sack their cities for prizes. Achilles says that he did not come because the Trojans had harmed him, but because Agamemnon and Menelaus sought satisfaction. The war is endangered when the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles causes Achilles to withdraw from the fighting.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Achilles, dishonoured by Agamemnon's seizure of his prize, withdraws from the fighting and asks his mother Thetis to seek Jove's help for the Trojans. Thetis petitions Jove, who promises to bring victory to the Trojans until the Achaeans restore Achilles's honour. Meanwhile, Ulysses returns Chryseis to Chryses and conducts a sacrifice to Apollo, after which the pestilence ends. Jove's secret promise leads to a quarrel with Juno, but Vulcan calms the gods, who feast together on Olympus.

l: Achilles, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Achilles weeps beside the sea because Agamemnon has dishonoured him and taken his prize. He asks Thetis to persuade Jove to aid the Trojans and remains beside his ships, refusing the assembly and battle while nursing his anger.

l: Thetis, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Thetis rises from the sea to comfort Achilles and promises to ask Jove for help. After twelve days she goes to Olympus, clasps Jove's knees, and persuades him to grant victory to the Trojans until Achilles receives his due.

l: Jove, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Jove promises Thetis that he will bring about victory for the Trojans until the Achaeans honour Achilles. His promise troubles him because he expects Juno to quarrel with him, but he confirms it by bowing his head.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Agamemnon refuses Chryses's request to ransom Chryseis and sends him away roughly. He later takes Briseis, whom the Achaeans had awarded to Achilles, thereby dishonouring Achilles.

l: Chryseis, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Chryseis is chosen as Agamemnon's share of the spoil from Thebe. Ulysses returns her to her father at Chryse, where she is received gladly.

l: Chryses, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Chryses, priest of Apollo, comes to the Achaean ships with a ransom for Chryseis and prays after Agamemnon rejects him. He receives Chryseis back from Ulysses and leads the sacrifice and prayer that end the pestilence.

l: Apollo, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Apollo sends a deadly pestilence upon the Achaeans after hearing Chryses's prayer. He hears Chryses's later prayer at Chryse, and the pestilence is stayed.

l: Ulysses, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Ulysses takes Chryseis and the hecatomb to Chryse on Agamemnon's orders. He leads Chryseis to the altar and delivers her to Chryses before the sacrifice to Apollo.

l: Juno, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Juno suspects that Thetis has persuaded Jove to aid Achilles and reproaches him for keeping counsel from her. Jove threatens her, and she becomes frightened and sits silently; she later smiles at Vulcan's words and accepts the nectar he gives her.

l: Briseis, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Briseis is the daughter of Briseus and is awarded to Achilles by the Achaeans. Agamemnon's heralds take her from Achilles's tent.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: The Achaeans sack Thebe and divide its spoil, choosing Chryseis for Agamemnon and Briseis for Achilles. They suffer Apollo's pestilence, return Chryseis with sacrifices, and are later threatened with defeat until they restore Achilles's due.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: The Trojans are to receive Jove's aid after Thetis's petition. Jove intends for them to gain victory until the Achaeans honour Achilles.

l: the gods, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: The gods return to Olympus after feasting among the Ethiopians. They stand before Jove, are disquieted by his quarrel with Juno, and later feast, listen to Apollo's lyre and the Muses, and retire to their own abodes.

l: Olympus, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Olympus is where Jove sits on its topmost ridges and where Thetis petitions him. It reels when Jove bows his head to confirm his promise.

l: the sea, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Achilles weeps and prays beside the hoar sea. Thetis rises from its depths to comfort him and later returns to it after securing Jove's promise.

l: Chryse, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Chryse is reached by Ulysses's ship, where Chryseis is returned to Chryses. A hecatomb is sacrificed there, and Apollo's pestilence is stayed.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Achilles remains beside the ships of the Achaeans instead of attending the assembly or fighting. Thetis asks Jove to let the Achaeans be hemmed in at their sterns and perish on the sea-shore.

l: Briseis' prize, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: The prize is the woman awarded to a warrior from the spoil. Agamemnon takes Achilles's prize by force, causing Achilles to appeal to Thetis and withdraw from battle.

l: hecatomb, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: The hecatomb is sent with Chryseis to Chryse as an offering to Apollo. It is arranged around the altar, sacrificed, roasted, eaten, and accompanied by song and prayer.

l: Apollo's pestilence, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: The pestilence is sent by Apollo after Chryses prays against the Achaeans. It ends when Chryses receives Chryseis back and offers sacrifice and prayer to Apollo.

l: Achilles’ anger, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: Achilles's anger begins with Agamemnon's seizure of his prize. He continues to nurse it beside his ships, refusing to join the assembly or fight.

l: the sacrifice to Apollo, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: The sacrifice to Apollo is conducted at Chryse after Chryseis is returned. Chryses and the Achaeans pray, burn the thigh-bones, feast, and hymn Apollo, after which the pestilence is stopped.

l: the Trojan War, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: The unit concerns the conflict between the Achaeans and the Trojans and shows how Achilles's withdrawal affects it. Jove promises that the Trojans will gain victory until the Achaeans make amends to Achilles.

l: Agamemnon's insult and seizure of Achilles' prize, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: The dishonour of Achilles occurs when Agamemnon takes the prize awarded to him. Achilles asks Thetis to secure divine compensation, and Jove agrees to aid the Trojans until the Achaeans restore Achilles's honour.

l: the promise of Jove, The Iliad, to go. Then Achilles went all alone by the side of the hoar sea,
s: The promise of Jove is made to Thetis after she clasps his knees and asks him to help Achilles. Jove confirms it by inclining his head and promises victory to the Trojans until the Achaeans give Achilles his due.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, BOOK II.
s: Jove sends a lying dream to Agamemnon, promising that the Achaeans will take Troy, and Agamemnon calls the chiefs and army to assembly. When Agamemnon tests the army by proposing that they sail home, the Achaeans rush toward their ships until Juno sends Minerva to stop them. Ulysses restores order, beats Thersites for insulting Agamemnon, and urges the army to remain until Troy falls. Nestor and Ulysses recall the prophecy that the Achaeans will fight for nine years and take Troy in the tenth, after which Agamemnon orders preparations for battle.

Jove, thinking how to honor Achilles, sends a lying dream to Agamemnon and promises through it that the Achaeans will take Troy. He later remains the source of the prophecy that the Achaeans will succeed, though the dream conceals his plan for further fighting.

l: Lying Dream, The Iliad, BOOK II.
s: The Lying Dream goes to Agamemnon's tent in the likeness of Nestor son of Neleus and tells him that Jove commands the Achaeans to arm themselves because Troy will fall. It leaves Agamemnon believing that he will take Priam's city that same day.

Agamemnon receives the lying dream, summons the elders and the wider army, and proposes to test the Achaeans by telling them to sail home. After Ulysses restores order, Agamemnon orders the army to eat, arm itself, inspect its horses and chariots, and prepare for battle.
Achilles is described as a man whom Agamemnon has offended by taking his prize. He is said to be a better man than Agamemnon and to have endured the insult without fighting back.

Nestor son of Neleus is honored by Agamemnon above his other councillors, and the Lying Dream takes his likeness. Nestor supports arming the Achaeans, urges Agamemnon to divide them by tribes and clans, and recalls the signs and prophecy concerning Troy.

The Achaeans gather in disorder for assembly and initially rush toward their ships when Agamemnon suggests returning home. Minerva and Ulysses stop their flight, and the Achaeans finally renew their resolve to remain and fight the Trojans.
The Trojans are presented as the enemy whose city the Achaeans seek to sack. Their allies from other places are said to have prevented Agamemnon from taking Troy during the preceding nine years.
Troy is the city that Agamemnon believes the Achaeans will take and that the army is urged to remain and attack. The prophecy recalled by Ulysses says that Troy will be taken in the tenth year.
The Argives are another name used for the Achaean forces. They are stirred by Agamemnon's proposal to sail home, then are recalled to assembly and urged by Ulysses and Nestor to continue the war.

The assembly is first convened for the elders at Nestor's ship and then for the whole army. It becomes disorderly when the people rush toward the ships, but Ulysses and the heralds restore silence so that counsel can be heard.

Minerva answers Juno's command and goes among the Achaeans to prevent them from drawing their ships into the sea. She speaks to Ulysses and later, in the likeness of a herald, helps keep the assembly quiet.

Ulysses refuses to launch his ship, accepts Agamemnon's ancestral staff, and persuades the chiefs and common soldiers to return to the assembly. He rebukes and beats Thersites, then recalls the prophecy of the nine years of fighting and the capture of Troy in the tenth.

Thersites openly insults Agamemnon, accuses him of taking prizes, and urges the Achaeans to sail home. Ulysses rebukes him, beats him with the staff, and drives him from speaking further in the assembly.
Priam is identified as the king whose city the Achaeans have come to attack. Agamemnon speaks of sacking the city of Priam, and Ulysses urges the army not to return before taking it.

Helen is described as the woman for whose sake many Achaeans have died at Troy far from their homes. Juno and Minerva warn that the Achaeans must not leave Priam and the Trojans the glory of still keeping her.

l: prophecy of Troy’s fall, The Iliad, BOOK II.
s: At Aulis, Calchas interprets a serpent's killing of eight sparrows and their mother as a sign that the Achaeans will fight for nine years and take Troy in the tenth. Ulysses invokes this prophecy to persuade the Achaeans to remain.

l: the Trojan War, The Iliad, BOOK II.
s: The Trojan War has lasted nine years in this unit, and the Achaeans remain far from their homes while their ships and equipment decay. Agamemnon orders them to prepare for another full day of battle against the Trojans.

l: return to Argos, The Iliad, BOOK II.
s: Agamemnon proposes that the Achaeans sail back to Argos because Troy has not yet been taken. The army briefly attempts to prepare its ships for the return, but Minerva and Ulysses stop the movement.

l: flight of the Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK II.
s: The flight of the Achaeans begins when Agamemnon tests them by urging them to sail home. They rush toward the ships, but Juno sends Minerva to prevent the flight, and Ulysses brings the army back to assembly.

l: the Achaean army, The Iliad, BOOK II.
s: The Achaean army gathers in great confusion, is disciplined by Ulysses, and is reminded of its oath, its long labor, and the prophecy of victory. Agamemnon then commands it to eat, arm itself, inspect its equipment, and join battle.

l: ships of the Achaeans, The Iliad, BOOK II.
s: The Achaean ships are the destination toward which the army rushes when it believes it will return home. Their timbers have rotted and their tackling is no longer sound after nine years, but Minerva and Ulysses prevent the army from launching them.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the
s: The Achaeans return to their ships, eat after making sacrifices, and pray to live through the fighting. Agamemnon sacrifices a bull to Jove and asks for Troy, Priam’s palace, and Hector to be destroyed, but Jove does not grant his prayer. Nestor urges the chiefs to gather the people, and Agamemnon orders the mustering of the host. Minerva encourages the Achaeans, who assemble in great numbers and prepare to attack the Trojans.

l: Achaeans, The Iliad, Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the
s: The Achaeans hurry to their ships, light fires, eat, and offer sacrifices while praying to survive the fighting. They gather on the plain of the Scamander in great numbers, encouraged by Minerva, and prepare to charge and destroy the Trojans.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the
s: Agamemnon sacrifices a fat five-year-old bull to Jove and invites the leading princes and elders to join him. He prays for Priam’s palace to be destroyed, for Hector to be pierced by his sword, and for many of Hector’s comrades to die. He then orders the criers to summon the people to assembly.

l: Nestor, The Iliad, Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the
s: Nestor urges Agamemnon not to delay in conversation but to summon the people and begin fighting. Agamemnon follows his advice.

l: Jove, The Iliad, Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the
s: Jove accepts Agamemnon’s sacrifice but does not grant his prayer. Instead, he continues to increase the Achaeans’ toil.

l: Minerva, The Iliad, Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the
s: Minerva moves furiously among the Achaean hosts with her ageless, deathless aegis. She urges the Achaeans forward and gives each one courage to fight without ceasing.

l: Trojans, The Iliad, Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the
s: The Trojans are the enemy whom the Achaeans assemble to charge and destroy.

l: battle, The Iliad, Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the
s: The coming battle is prepared through sacrifices, prayers, mustering, and the arrangement of the chiefs’ men. The Achaeans are eager to fight, and Agamemnon directs their forces toward an immediate attack.

l: the Achaean mustering, The Iliad, Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the
s: The Achaean mustering begins when Agamemnon sends criers to summon the people to assembly. The chiefs choose and marshal their men, while the assembled forces pour from the ships and tents onto the plain.

l: the Achaean army, The Iliad, Thus he spoke, and the Achaeans roared applause. As when the
s: The Achaean army is shown as vast and densely assembled, with its armour flashing as it advances. Its chiefs arrange the troops, Agamemnon stands out among the heroes, and Minerva strengthens the army’s courage for battle.

l: The Iliad, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: The unit catalogs the chiefs, peoples, territories, and ships of the Danaans, including Agamemnon, Menelaus, Diomed, Nestor, Ulysses, and Achilles. It describes the Achaeans’ advance, noting that Achilles and his Myrmidons remain apart because of his quarrel with Agamemnon, while Ajax son of Telamon is foremost among the fighting men during Achilles’ absence. Iris warns the Trojans of the advancing host, and Hector organizes the Trojans and their allies outside the city. The Trojan forces are then listed, including Aeneas’s Dardanians and the Lycian contingent led by Sarpedon and Glaucus.

l: Muses, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: The Muses are invoked to recount the chiefs and peoples of the Danaans because they are goddesses who see all things. They are also said to have punished Thamyris by taking away his power of song.

l: Danaans, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: The Danaans are listed by their regional contingents, chiefs, territories, and ships. Their host advances across the plain toward the city, with the earth groaning beneath its movement.

l: Ajax son of Oileus, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Ajax son of Oileus commands the Locrians, who bring forty ships. He is smaller than Ajax son of Telamon and wears a linen breastplate, but he excels all the Hellenes and Achaeans in use of the spear.

l: Ajax son of Telamon, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Ajax son of Telamon brings twelve ships from Salamis and stations them beside the Athenians. He is the foremost of the fighting men while Achilles remains apart, though Achilles is said to excel him greatly.

l: Athens, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Athens is held by the people of Erechtheus and sends fifty ships under Menestheus. The Athenian contingent is stationed beside the ships brought from Salamis by Ajax son of Telamon.

l: Argos, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Argos and the surrounding territories send eighty ships under Diomed, Sthenelus, and Euryalus. Pelasgic Argos is separately listed among the lands whose people serve under Achilles.

l: Diomed, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Diomed commands the men of Argos, Tiryns, Hermione, Asine, Troezene, Eionae, Epidaurus, Aegina, and Mases. Sthenelus and Euryalus serve with him, but Diomed is chief over the whole contingent of eighty ships.

l: Mycenae, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Mycenae, together with Corinth, Cleonae, and other surrounding lands, sends a hundred ships. These forces are commanded by Agamemnon.

l: Agamemnon, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Agamemnon commands the hundred ships from Mycenae and neighboring territories. His force is described as the finest and most numerous, and he is the greatest king among the heroes, with the most men under him.

l: Sparta, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Sparta and the surrounding Lacedaemonian settlements send sixty ships under Menelaus. Their contingent is drawn up apart from the others.

l: Menelaus, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Menelaus commands the people of Sparta and neighboring Lacedaemonian settlements. He urges them to fight because he longs to avenge the toil and sorrow he suffered for Helen.

l: Helen, The Iliad, And now, O Muses, dwellers in the mansions of Olympus, tell
s: Helen is identified as the reason for Menelaus’s suffering and desire for revenge. Menelaus’s contingent fights in connection with the wrong he suffered for her sake.
